(﴿كالمُهْلِ﴾, "like molten brass") The discussion of it has already passed in Surat al-Dukhan. ﴿وتَكُونُ الجِبالُ كالعِهْنِ المَنفُوشِ﴾ [Al-Qari'a: 5] ("And the mountains will be like fluffed wool") as in al-Qari'a: when they are blown away, they fly in the air like fluffed wool when the wind scatters it. Al-Hasan said: the mountains move with the winds, then they crumble, then they become like wool, then they are blown away and become scattered dust.

The majority read (﴿ولا يَسْألُ﴾, "and no close friend will ask") in the active form, meaning: he will not ask him for help or benefit, knowing that he will not find that with him. Qatada said: he will not ask him about his condition, because it is evident. It was also said: he will not ask him to bear for him any part of his burdens, for he has despaired of that. It was also said: intercession. It was also said: *ḥamīman* ("a close friend") is in the accusative by the removal of *ʿan* ("about"), meaning: about a close friend, because of his preoccupation with what he is in.

Abu Haywa, Shayba, Abu Ja'far and al-Bazzi, with some difference of transmission from these three, read it in the passive form, meaning: he will not be asked to bring him, since each of the believer and the disbeliever has a sign by which he is recognized. It was also said: he will not be asked about the sins of his close friend, so that he may be taken to account for them.

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ ("they will be made to see them"): a resumption of speech. Ibn ʿAbbas said: on the gathering-place, the close friend sees his close friend, then he flees from him because of his preoccupation with himself. It was also said: they are made to see them in the Fire. It was also said: they are made to see them, so they have no need to ask or to request. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that "they are made to see them" is a qualifying clause, meaning: close friends who are made to see one another, turning them away. End of quotation. ﴿حَمِيمٌ حَمِيمًا﴾ ("close friend ... close friend"): both are indefinite nouns in a negative context, so they are general, and for this reason the pronoun was made plural. Qatada read ﴿يُبْصِرُونَهم﴾ ("they make them see") with *tashdid* removed and with the *ṣad* vowelled with kasra, meaning: the believer sees the disbeliever in the Fire; this was said by Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: the disbeliever sees the one who misled him in the Fire, as a lesson, as vengeance, and as grief.

﴿يَوَدُّ المُجْرِمُ﴾ ("the guilty one would wish"): that is, the disbeliever, though it may include the sinful believer who is punished. The majority read *min ʿadhābi* as an idafa (construct). Abu Haywa read it with *fatḥa* on the final vowel. (﴿وصاحِبَتِهِ﴾, "and his spouse") his wife. (﴿وفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾, "and his close kin") his nearest relatives. (﴿تُؤْوِيهِ﴾, "that shelters him") that takes him in, by belonging to it, or seeking refuge with it in calamities.

﴿ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ ("and then rescues him") is conjoined to (﴿يَفْتَدِي﴾, "would ransom himself"), meaning: rescues him by ransoming, or the ones mentioned before. Al-Zuhri read *tu'wīhi* and *tunjīhi* with both *hā'*s vowelled with *ḍamma*. (﴿كَلّا﴾, "No!") a rebuke to their wish to ransom themselves, and an alert that it will not benefit. (﴿إنَّها﴾, "Indeed it") the pronoun refers to the matter (the story), and ﴿لَظى نَزّاعَةً﴾ ("the Blaze, plucking out") is an explanation of it, or of the Fire, which is indicated by the word *ʿadhāb* ("punishment") in ﴿عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ﴾ ("the punishment of that day"). ﴿لَظى﴾ ("the Blaze") is a substitute for the pronoun, and ﴿نَزّاعَةً﴾ ("plucking out") is the predicate of *inna*, or the predicate of an inchoative, and ﴿لَظى﴾ is the predicate of *inna*, meaning: it is plucking out; or it is a substitute for ﴿لَظى﴾, or a predicate after a predicate. All of this has been mentioned, on the reading of the majority with the *rafʿ* ("nominative") of "plucking out". Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that it be an ambiguous pronoun explained by the predicate. End of quotation. I do not know what this hidden pronoun is that the predicate explains; this is not one of the positions in which a single noun explains a pronoun. Were it not that he mentioned after this "or the pronoun of the matter", I would have interpreted his words in that sense. Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Haywa, al-Za'farani, Ibn Miqsam, Hafs, and al-Yazidi in his selection read "plucking out" with *naṣb* ("accusative"). Then it is fixed that ﴿لَظى﴾ is the predicate of *inna*, and the pronoun in *innahā* refers to the Fire which is indicated by "punishment". "Plucking out" is in the accusative as a qualifying state, either emphasizing or specifying, and the element governing it is ﴿لَظى﴾, although it governs it only insofar as there is in it the sense of blazing, just as the proper name governs the adverb in the poet's words:

"I am Abu al-Minhal, at times."

That is: famous at times. Or it is in the accusative of specification for exaggeration (*li-l-tahwīl*); this was said by al-Zamakhshari, and he seems to mean the cutting-off (of the qualifier). So the accusative in it is like the nominative in it, if you supply "he" as a pronoun, so you supply it here, I mean "calls", that is: in reality God creates in it speech, just as He creates it in the limbs; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and others, "calling them by their names and their fathers' names". Al-Zamakhshari said: and as He created it in the tree. End of quotation. He thus did not abandon the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). Al-Khalil said: it is a metaphor for its summoning them, and what it inflicts on them of its punishment. Tha'lab said: it destroys; the Arabs say: *daʿā Allāhu*, meaning: God destroyed you; al-Khalil related this from the Arabs. The poet said:

"Nights when passion calls me, and I answer it, and the eyes of the one I love look at me with tenderness."

And another said:

"It rose up to be seen, and every wide path was made dear to it by pasture and open land."

He describes an ostrich; *ṭabāhu* means: called it. Passion and pasture cannot literally call, but since in them there is something that attracts, they became callers figuratively. It was also said: ﴿تَدْعُو﴾ ("calls") means: the guardians of Hell, whose calling is attributed to it.

﴿مَن أدْبَرَ﴾ ("whoever turned his back") from the truth, ﴿وتَوَلّى﴾ ("and turned away"), ﴿وجَمَعَ فَأوْعى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded"): that is, gathered wealth, placed it in a container, hoarded it, and did not pay God's right in it. This is an indication of wealthy disbelievers. Al-Hakim said: ʿAbdullah ibn Hakim would not tie up his purse, and he said: I heard God say: ﴿وجَمَعَ فَأوْعى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded").

﴿إنَّ الإنْسانَ﴾ ("Indeed, man") is a generic noun, and for this reason an exception is made from it: ﴿إلّا المُصَلِّينَ﴾ ("except those who pray"). It was also said: the reference is to the disbelievers. Tha'lab said: Muhammad ibn ʿAbdullah ibn Tahir said to me: What is *al-halaʿ* (anxiety)? I said: God has already explained it, and there can be no explanation clearer than His explanation, which is: when evil reaches him he shows extreme distress, and when good reaches him he is stingy with it and withholds it from people. End of quotation.

Since extreme distress and withholding are firmly established in man, it is as if he were created carried upon them, like His words: ﴿خُلِقَ الإنْسانُ مِن عَجَلٍ﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 37] ("Man was created of haste"). And *al-khayr* ("good") means wealth.

﴿إلّا المُصَلِّينَ﴾ ("except those who pray"): an exception from "man", as we have said; for this reason He described them with what He described them, namely patience under hardships, and the beautiful attributes which they practise. The majority read ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ﴾ ("over their prayer") in the singular; al-Hasan read it in the plural. And *daymūmatuhā* ("constancy in it"): the majority said: persistence in it. Ibn Mas'ud said: its performance at its time. ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir said: they remain in it and do not turn right or left, and from this comes "lasting wealth". Al-Zamakhshari said: their constancy in it is that they persist in performing it and do not occupy themselves away from it with anything; and their guarding of it is that they observe the completion of the ablution for it and its times, and they establish its pillars and complete it with its sunnas and its performance, and they protect it from being nullified by the sins that accompany it; and constancy returns to the prayers themselves and to the guarding of their states. End of quotation. This is his answer to the question: (If you say): how did He say ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ دائِمُونَ﴾ ("who are constant in their prayer") and then say ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ يُحافِظُونَ﴾ ("who guard their prayer")? I say: constancy in a thing and guarding it are one thing; but since prayer is the pillar of Islam, emphasis was carried to the utmost in it, so it was mentioned first and last among the qualities of Islam mentioned in this surah, to make known its rank among the pillars upon which Islam is built. The attributes that come after these have already been explained, and most of them are in Surat Qad Aflaha al-Mu'minun ("The believers have prospered"). The majority read ﴿بِشَهادَتِهِمْ﴾ ("in their testimonies") in the singular. Al-Sulami, Abu ʿAmr and Hafs read it in the plural.

﴿ذِي المَعارِجِ﴾: *al-ma'arij* means ascents or stairways, and here it is a metaphor. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada said: in ranks, favours and praiseworthy attributes. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: *al-ma'arij* are the heavens, in which the angels ascend from one heaven to another. Al-Hasan said: they are the steps up to heaven. It was also said: *al-ma'arij* are the upper chambers, meaning that He made them for His friends in Paradise.

(﴿تَعْرُجُ﴾) The reading of the majority is with the *ta'* (feminine form). ʿAbdullah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Miqsam and Za'ida from al-A'mash read it with the *ya'* (masculine form). (﴿والرُّوحُ﴾, "and the Spirit") The majority said: it is Gabriel, singled out for mention as an honour, and it is placed after the angels here, whereas it is placed before them in His words: ﴿يَوْمَ يَقُومُ الرُّوحُ والمَلائِكَةُ صَفًّا﴾ [An-Naba': 38] ("On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks"). Mujahid said: they are angels who guard the angels who guard the children of Adam; the guarding angels do not see them, just as we do not see our guardians. It was also said: the Spirit is an angel other than Gabriel, of great size. Abu Salih said: a creation in the form of humans, but they are not humans. Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb said: it is the spirit of the dead person at the moment it is taken. The pronoun ﴿إلَيْهِ﴾ ("to Him") refers to Allah, i.e. to His Throne, and to where His command descends from. It was also said: ﴿إلَيْهِ﴾ means to the place where they dwell, which is in the heaven, since it is the place of His goodness and honour. The apparent meaning is that they ascend in a day of your days, and the measure of the distance, if a human were to ascend it, is fifty thousand years. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Ishaq, and a group of the skilled scholars, among them the judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id. If the one ascending is an angel, Mujahid said: the distance is from the bottom of the seventh earth to the Throne. And whoever takes the Spirit to be a class of living creatures said: Wahb said: the distance is from the surface of the earth to the farthest end of the Throne. ʿIkrima and al-Hakam said: He meant the duration of this world, for it is fifty thousand years, and no one knows how much of it has passed and how much remains; that is, they ascend within the span of the world and the continuance of this structure. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: it is the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: its length is that number, and this is the apparent meaning of what has come in the hadith about the one who withholds zakat, for he said: "On a day whose measure is fifty thousand years." Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: He determined it, in its calamities, its terror and its severity, to be that number for the disbelievers. A hadith says: "It will be light for the believer, until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer." ʿIkrima said: the measure of the time in which the reckoning is concluded is the amount of time that would be needed to judge with justice over fifty thousand years of the days of this world. Al-Hasan said something similar. It was also said: the number is not meant literally; what is meant is the length of the standing on the Day of Resurrection and the hardships therein. The Arabs describe days of hardship as long, and days of joy as short. A poet describing days of joy and happiness said:

"And a day that, like the shadow of a spear, its length was shortened by the blood of the wineskin and the clashing of the lutes."

The apparent view is that His words "in a day" are connected to (﴿تَعْرُجُ﴾, "ascend"). It was also said that they are connected to (﴿دافِعٍ﴾, "averter"), and the clause "ascend" is a parenthetical insertion. Since they had asked for the hastening of the punishment, and that asking was in the manner of mockery and denial, and they had been promised it, He commanded him to be patient. As for the one who took (﴿سَألَ سائِلٌ﴾, "asked") to mean "flowing", the meaning is that it has come close to occurring. The pronoun in ﴿يَرَوْنَهُ﴾ ("they see it") refers to the punishment, or to the day if it is meant to be the Day of Resurrection. This regarding it as far away is, on their part, a form of denial by way of impossibility.

﴿ونَراهُ قَرِيبًا﴾ ("and We see it near"): that is, easy for Our power, not far from Us and not unattainable. Everything that is coming is near. Nearness and farness here concern possibility, not distance.

﴿يَوْمَ تَكُونُ﴾ ("on a day when it will be"): it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: it occurs on the day when ... ; or (﴿يَوْمَ تَكُونُ السَّماءُ كالمُهْلِ﴾, "on the day when the sky will be like molten brass") is such-and-such; or it is governed by (﴿قَرِيبًا﴾, "near"); or it is a substitute for the pronoun in "We see it" if that refers to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is a substitute for "in a day" according to the one who connected it to (﴿واقِعٍ﴾, "befalling"). End of quotation. This is not permissible, because "in a day", although it is in a position of accusative, cannot have an accusative substitute, since this is not among the positions which are observed in following words (*tawabi'*), for the preposition in it is not superfluous, nor is it treated as superfluous like *rubba*. The observance of position is only permitted with a superfluous preposition, as in the poem:

"O sons of Lubayna, you are not [a fist] in hand, except a hand that has no arm."

For this reason it is not permitted to say: "I passed by Zayd the tailor," observing the position of "by Zayd"; nor "I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr," nor "I was angry at Zayd and Jaʿfar," nor "I passed by ʿAmr, your brother," observing the position. (If you say): the vowel on *yawma* ("day") is a vowel of construction (*bina'*), not a vowel of grammatical inflection (*i'rab*), so it is in the genitive like "in a day." (I reply): its construction is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans, because it is attached to an inflected noun; but it is permitted according to the school of the Kufans. Al-Zamakhshari's statement would then be consistent with their school, if he had this in mind and intended it.

(﴿كالمُهْلِ﴾, "like molten brass") The discussion of it has already passed in Surat al-Dukhan. ﴿وتَكُونُ الجِبالُ كالعِهْنِ المَنفُوشِ﴾ [Al-Qari'a: 5] ("And the mountains will be like fluffed wool") as in al-Qari'a: when they are blown away, they fly in the air like fluffed wool when the wind scatters it. Al-Hasan said: the mountains move with the winds, then they crumble, then they become like wool, then they are blown away and become scattered dust.

The majority read (﴿ولا يَسْألُ﴾, "and no close friend will ask") in the active form, meaning: he will not ask him for help or benefit, knowing that he will not find that with him. Qatada said: he will not ask him about his condition, because it is evident. It was also said: he will not ask him to bear for him any part of his burdens, for he has despaired of that. It was also said: intercession. It was also said: *ḥamīman* ("a close friend") is in the accusative by the removal of *ʿan* ("about"), meaning: about a close friend, because of his preoccupation with what he is in.

Abu Haywa, Shayba, Abu Ja'far and al-Bazzi, with some difference of transmission from these three, read it in the passive form, meaning: he will not be asked to bring him, since each of the believer and the disbeliever has a sign by which he is recognized. It was also said: he will not be asked about the sins of his close friend, so that he may be taken to account for them.

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ ("they will be made to see them"): a resumption of speech. Ibn ʿAbbas said: on the gathering-place, the close friend sees his close friend, then he flees from him because of his preoccupation with himself. It was also said: they are made to see them in the Fire. It was also said: they are made to see them, so they have no need to ask or to request. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that "they are made to see them" is a qualifying clause, meaning: close friends who are made to see one another, turning them away. End of quotation. ﴿حَمِيمٌ حَمِيمًا﴾ ("close friend ... close friend"): both are indefinite nouns in a negative context, so they are general, and for this reason the pronoun was made plural. Qatada read ﴿يُبْصِرُونَهم﴾ ("they make them see") with *tashdid* removed and with the *ṣad* vowelled with kasra, meaning: the believer sees the disbeliever in the Fire; this was said by Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: the disbeliever sees the one who misled him in the Fire, as a lesson, as vengeance, and as grief.

﴿يَوَدُّ المُجْرِمُ﴾ ("the guilty one would wish"): that is, the disbeliever, though it may include the sinful believer who is punished. The majority read *min ʿadhābi* as an idafa (construct). Abu Haywa read it with *fatḥa* on the final vowel. (﴿وصاحِبَتِهِ﴾, "and his spouse") his wife. (﴿وفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾, "and his close kin") his nearest relatives. (﴿تُؤْوِيهِ﴾, "that shelters him") that takes him in, by belonging to it, or seeking refuge with it in calamities.

﴿ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ ("and then rescues him") is conjoined to (﴿يَفْتَدِي﴾, "would ransom himself"), meaning: rescues him by ransoming, or the ones mentioned before. Al-Zuhri read *tu'wīhi* and *tunjīhi* with both *hā'*s vowelled with *ḍamma*. (﴿كَلّا﴾, "No!") a rebuke to their wish to ransom themselves, and an alert that it will not benefit. (﴿إنَّها﴾, "Indeed it") the pronoun refers to the matter (the story), and ﴿لَظى نَزّاعَةً﴾ ("the Blaze, plucking out") is an explanation of it, or of the Fire, which is indicated by the word *ʿadhāb* ("punishment") in ﴿عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ﴾ ("the punishment of that day"). ﴿لَظى﴾ ("the Blaze") is a substitute for the pronoun, and ﴿نَزّاعَةً﴾ ("plucking out") is the predicate of *inna*, or the predicate of an inchoative, and ﴿لَظى﴾ is the predicate of *inna*, meaning: it is plucking out; or it is a substitute for ﴿لَظى﴾, or a predicate after a predicate. All of this has been mentioned, on the reading of the majority with the *rafʿ* ("nominative") of "plucking out". Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that it be an ambiguous pronoun explained by the predicate. End of quotation. I do not know what this hidden pronoun is that the predicate explains; this is not one of the positions in which a single noun explains a pronoun. Were it not that he mentioned after this "or the pronoun of the matter", I would have interpreted his words in that sense. Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Haywa, al-Za'farani, Ibn Miqsam, Hafs, and al-Yazidi in his selection read "plucking out" with *naṣb* ("accusative"). Then it is fixed that ﴿لَظى﴾ is the predicate of *inna*, and the pronoun in *innahā* refers to the Fire which is indicated by "punishment". "Plucking out" is in the accusative as a qualifying state, either emphasizing or specifying, and the element governing it is ﴿لَظى﴾, although it governs it only insofar as there is in it the sense of blazing, just as the proper name governs the adverb in the poet's words:

"I am Abu al-Minhal, at times."

That is: famous at times. Or it is in the accusative of specification for exaggeration (*li-l-tahwīl*); this was said by al-Zamakhshari, and he seems to mean the cutting-off (of the qualifier). So the accusative in it is like the nominative in it, if you supply "he" as a pronoun, so you supply it here, I mean "calls", that is: in reality God creates in it speech, just as He creates it in the limbs; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and others, "calling them by their names and their fathers' names". Al-Zamakhshari said: and as He created it in the tree. End of quotation. He thus did not abandon the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). Al-Khalil said: it is a metaphor for its summoning them, and what it inflicts on them of its punishment. Tha'lab said: it destroys; the Arabs say: *daʿā Allāhu*, meaning: God destroyed you; al-Khalil related this from the Arabs. The poet said:

"Nights when passion calls me, and I answer it, and the eyes of the one I love look at me with tenderness."

And another said:

"It rose up to be seen, and every wide path was made dear to it by pasture and open land."

He describes an ostrich; *ṭabāhu* means: called it. Passion and pasture cannot literally call, but since in them there is something that attracts, they became callers figuratively. It was also said: ﴿تَدْعُو﴾ ("calls") means: the guardians of Hell, whose calling is attributed to it.

﴿مَن أدْبَرَ﴾ ("whoever turned his back") from the truth, ﴿وتَوَلّى﴾ ("and turned away"), ﴿وجَمَعَ فَأوْعى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded"): that is, gathered wealth, placed it in a container, hoarded it, and did not pay God's right in it. This is an indication of wealthy disbelievers. Al-Hakim said: ʿAbdullah ibn Hakim would not tie up his purse, and he said: I heard God say: ﴿وجَمَعَ فَأوْعى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded").

﴿إنَّ الإنْسانَ﴾ ("Indeed, man") is a generic noun, and for this reason an exception is made from it: ﴿إلّا المُصَلِّينَ﴾ ("except those who pray"). It was also said: the reference is to the disbelievers. Tha'lab said: Muhammad ibn ʿAbdullah ibn Tahir said to me: What is *al-halaʿ* (anxiety)? I said: God has already explained it, and there can be no explanation clearer than His explanation, which is: when evil reaches him he shows extreme distress, and when good reaches him he is stingy with it and withholds it from people. End of quotation.

Since extreme distress and withholding are firmly established in man, it is as if he were created carried upon them, like His words: ﴿خُلِقَ الإنْسانُ مِن عَجَلٍ﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 37] ("Man was created of haste"). And *al-khayr* ("good") means wealth.

﴿إلّا المُصَلِّينَ﴾ ("except those who pray"): an exception from "man", as we have said; for this reason He described them with what He described them, namely patience under hardships, and the beautiful attributes which they practise. The majority read ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ﴾ ("over their prayer") in the singular; al-Hasan read it in the plural. And *daymūmatuhā* ("constancy in it"): the majority said: persistence in it. Ibn Mas'ud said: its performance at its time. ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir said: they remain in it and do not turn right or left, and from this comes "lasting wealth". Al-Zamakhshari said: their constancy in it is that they persist in performing it and do not occupy themselves away from it with anything; and their guarding of it is that they observe the completion of the ablution for it and its times, and they establish its pillars and complete it with its sunnas and its performance, and they protect it from being nullified by the sins that accompany it; and constancy returns to the prayers themselves and to the guarding of their states. End of quotation. This is his answer to the question: (If you say): how did He say ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ دائِمُونَ﴾ ("who are constant in their prayer") and then say ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ يُحافِظُونَ﴾ ("who guard their prayer")? I say: constancy in a thing and guarding it are one thing; but since prayer is the pillar of Islam, emphasis was carried to the utmost in it, so it was mentioned first and last among the qualities of Islam mentioned in this surah, to make known its rank among the pillars upon which Islam is built. The attributes that come after these have already been explained, and most of them are in Surat Qad Aflaha al-Mu'minun ("The believers have prospered"). The majority read ﴿بِشَهادَتِهِمْ﴾ ("in their testimonies") in the singular. Al-Sulami, Abu ʿAmr and Hafs read it in the plural.

﴿ذِي المَعارِجِ﴾: *al-ma'arij* means ascents or stairways, and here it is a metaphor. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada said: in ranks, favours and praiseworthy attributes. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: *al-ma'arij* are the heavens, in which the angels ascend from one heaven to another. Al-Hasan said: they are the steps up to heaven. It was also said: *al-ma'arij* are the upper chambers, meaning that He made them for His friends in Paradise.

(﴿تَعْرُجُ﴾) The reading of the majority is with the *ta'* (feminine form). ʿAbdullah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Miqsam and Za'ida from al-A'mash read it with the *ya'* (masculine form). (﴿والرُّوحُ﴾, "and the Spirit") The majority said: it is Gabriel, singled out for mention as an honour, and it is placed after the angels here, whereas it is placed before them in His words: ﴿يَوْمَ يَقُومُ الرُّوحُ والمَلائِكَةُ صَفًّا﴾ [An-Naba': 38] ("On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks"). Mujahid said: they are angels who guard the angels who guard the children of Adam; the guarding angels do not see them, just as we do not see our guardians. It was also said: the Spirit is an angel other than Gabriel, of great size. Abu Salih said: a creation in the form of humans, but they are not humans. Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb said: it is the spirit of the dead person at the moment it is taken. The pronoun ﴿إلَيْهِ﴾ ("to Him") refers to Allah, i.e. to His Throne, and to where His command descends from. It was also said: ﴿إلَيْهِ﴾ means to the place where they dwell, which is in the heaven, since it is the place of His goodness and honour. The apparent meaning is that they ascend in a day of your days, and the measure of the distance, if a human were to ascend it, is fifty thousand years. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Ishaq, and a group of the skilled scholars, among them the judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id. If the one ascending is an angel, Mujahid said: the distance is from the bottom of the seventh earth to the Throne. And whoever takes the Spirit to be a class of living creatures said: Wahb said: the distance is from the surface of the earth to the farthest end of the Throne. ʿIkrima and al-Hakam said: He meant the duration of this world, for it is fifty thousand years, and no one knows how much of it has passed and how much remains; that is, they ascend within the span of the world and the continuance of this structure. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: it is the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: its length is that number, and this is the apparent meaning of what has come in the hadith about the one who withholds zakat, for he said: "On a day whose measure is fifty thousand years." Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: He determined it, in its calamities, its terror and its severity, to be that number for the disbelievers. A hadith says: "It will be light for the believer, until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer." ʿIkrima said: the measure of the time in which the reckoning is concluded is the amount of time that would be needed to judge with justice over fifty thousand years of the days of this world. Al-Hasan said something similar. It was also said: the number is not meant literally; what is meant is the length of the standing on the Day of Resurrection and the hardships therein. The Arabs describe days of hardship as long, and days of joy as short. A poet describing days of joy and happiness said:

"And a day that, like the shadow of a spear, its length was shortened by the blood of the wineskin and the clashing of the lutes."

The apparent view is that His words "in a day" are connected to (﴿تَعْرُجُ﴾, "ascend"). It was also said that they are connected to (﴿دافِعٍ﴾, "averter"), and the clause "ascend" is a parenthetical insertion. Since they had asked for the hastening of the punishment, and that asking was in the manner of mockery and denial, and they had been promised it, He commanded him to be patient. As for the one who took (﴿سَألَ سائِلٌ﴾, "asked") to mean "flowing", the meaning is that it has come close to occurring. The pronoun in ﴿يَرَوْنَهُ﴾ ("they see it") refers to the punishment, or to the day if it is meant to be the Day of Resurrection. This regarding it as far away is, on their part, a form of denial by way of impossibility.

﴿ونَراهُ قَرِيبًا﴾ ("and We see it near"): that is, easy for Our power, not far from Us and not unattainable. Everything that is coming is near. Nearness and farness here concern possibility, not distance.

﴿يَوْمَ تَكُونُ﴾ ("on a day when it will be"): it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: it occurs on the day when ... ; or (﴿يَوْمَ تَكُونُ السَّماءُ كالمُهْلِ﴾, "on the day when the sky will be like molten brass") is such-and-such; or it is governed by (﴿قَرِيبًا﴾, "near"); or it is a substitute for the pronoun in "We see it" if that refers to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is a substitute for "in a day" according to the one who connected it to (﴿واقِعٍ﴾, "befalling"). End of quotation. This is not permissible, because "in a day", although it is in a position of accusative, cannot have an accusative substitute, since this is not among the positions which are observed in following words (*tawabi'*), for the preposition in it is not superfluous, nor is it treated as superfluous like *rubba*. The observance of position is only permitted with a superfluous preposition, as in the poem:

"O sons of Lubayna, you are not [a fist] in hand, except a hand that has no arm."

For this reason it is not permitted to say: "I passed by Zayd the tailor," observing the position of "by Zayd"; nor "I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr," nor "I was angry at Zayd and Jaʿfar," nor "I passed by ʿAmr, your brother," observing the position. (If you say): the vowel on *yawma* ("day") is a vowel of construction (*bina'*), not a vowel of grammatical inflection (*i'rab*), so it is in the genitive like "in a day." (I reply): its construction is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans, because it is attached to an inflected noun; but it is permitted according to the school of the Kufans. Al-Zamakhshari's statement would then be consistent with their school, if he had this in mind and intended it.

(﴿كالمُهْلِ﴾, "like molten brass") The discussion of it has already passed in Surat al-Dukhan. ﴿وتَكُونُ الجِبالُ كالعِهْنِ المَنفُوشِ﴾ [Al-Qari'a: 5] ("And the mountains will be like fluffed wool") as in al-Qari'a: when they are blown away, they fly in the air like fluffed wool when the wind scatters it. Al-Hasan said: the mountains move with the winds, then they crumble, then they become like wool, then they are blown away and become scattered dust.

The majority read (﴿ولا يَسْألُ﴾, "and no close friend will ask") in the active form, meaning: he will not ask him for help or benefit, knowing that he will not find that with him. Qatada said: he will not ask him about his condition, because it is evident. It was also said: he will not ask him to bear for him any part of his burdens, for he has despaired of that. It was also said: intercession. It was also said: *ḥamīman* ("a close friend") is in the accusative by the removal of *ʿan* ("about"), meaning: about a close friend, because of his preoccupation with what he is in.

Abu Haywa, Shayba, Abu Ja'far and al-Bazzi, with some difference of transmission from these three, read it in the passive form, meaning: he will not be asked to bring him, since each of the believer and the disbeliever has a sign by which he is recognized. It was also said: he will not be asked about the sins of his close friend, so that he may be taken to account for them.

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ ("they will be made to see them"): a resumption of speech. Ibn ʿAbbas said: on the gathering-place, the close friend sees his close friend, then he flees from him because of his preoccupation with himself. It was also said: they are made to see them in the Fire. It was also said: they are made to see them, so they have no need to ask or to request. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that "they are made to see them" is a qualifying clause, meaning: close friends who are made to see one another, turning them away. End of quotation. ﴿حَمِيمٌ حَمِيمًا﴾ ("close friend ... close friend"): both are indefinite nouns in a negative context, so they are general, and for this reason the pronoun was made plural. Qatada read ﴿يُبْصِرُونَهم﴾ ("they make them see") with *tashdid* removed and with the *ṣad* vowelled with kasra, meaning: the believer sees the disbeliever in the Fire; this was said by Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: the disbeliever sees the one who misled him in the Fire, as a lesson, as vengeance, and as grief.

﴿يَوَدُّ المُجْرِمُ﴾ ("the guilty one would wish"): that is, the disbeliever, though it may include the sinful believer who is punished. The majority read *min ʿadhābi* as an idafa (construct). Abu Haywa read it with *fatḥa* on the final vowel. (﴿وصاحِبَتِهِ﴾, "and his spouse") his wife. (﴿وفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾, "and his close kin") his nearest relatives. (﴿تُؤْوِيهِ﴾, "that shelters him") that takes him in, by belonging to it, or seeking refuge with it in calamities.

﴿ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ ("and then rescues him") is conjoined to (﴿يَفْتَدِي﴾, "would ransom himself"), meaning: rescues him by ransoming, or the ones mentioned before. Al-Zuhri read *tu'wīhi* and *tunjīhi* with both *hā'*s vowelled with *ḍamma*. (﴿كَلّا﴾, "No!") a rebuke to their wish to ransom themselves, and an alert that it will not benefit. (﴿إنَّها﴾, "Indeed it") the pronoun refers to the matter (the story), and ﴿لَظى نَزّاعَةً﴾ ("the Blaze, plucking out") is an explanation of it, or of the Fire, which is indicated by the word *ʿadhāb* ("punishment") in ﴿عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ﴾ ("the punishment of that day"). ﴿لَظى﴾ ("the Blaze") is a substitute for the pronoun, and ﴿نَزّاعَةً﴾ ("plucking out") is the predicate of *inna*, or the predicate of an inchoative, and ﴿لَظى﴾ is the predicate of *inna*, meaning: it is plucking out; or it is a substitute for ﴿لَظى﴾, or a predicate after a predicate. All of this has been mentioned, on the reading of the majority with the *rafʿ* ("nominative") of "plucking out". Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that it be an ambiguous pronoun explained by the predicate. End of quotation. I do not know what this hidden pronoun is that the predicate explains; this is not one of the positions in which a single noun explains a pronoun. Were it not that he mentioned after this "or the pronoun of the matter", I would have interpreted his words in that sense. Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Haywa, al-Za'farani, Ibn Miqsam, Hafs, and al-Yazidi in his selection read "plucking out" with *naṣb* ("accusative"). Then it is fixed that ﴿لَظى﴾ is the predicate of *inna*, and the pronoun in *innahā* refers to the Fire which is indicated by "punishment". "Plucking out" is in the accusative as a qualifying state, either emphasizing or specifying, and the element governing it is ﴿لَظى﴾, although it governs it only insofar as there is in it the sense of blazing, just as the proper name governs the adverb in the poet's words:

"I am Abu al-Minhal, at times."

That is: famous at times. Or it is in the accusative of specification for exaggeration (*li-l-tahwīl*); this was said by al-Zamakhshari, and he seems to mean the cutting-off (of the qualifier). So the accusative in it is like the nominative in it, if you supply "he" as a pronoun, so you supply it here, I mean "calls", that is: in reality God creates in it speech, just as He creates it in the limbs; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and others, "calling them by their names and their fathers' names". Al-Zamakhshari said: and as He created it in the tree. End of quotation. He thus did not abandon the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). Al-Khalil said: it is a metaphor for its summoning them, and what it inflicts on them of its punishment. Tha'lab said: it destroys; the Arabs say: *daʿā Allāhu*, meaning: God destroyed you; al-Khalil related this from the Arabs. The poet said:

"Nights when passion calls me, and I answer it, and the eyes of the one I love look at me with tenderness."

And another said:

"It rose up to be seen, and every wide path was made dear to it by pasture and open land."

He describes an ostrich; *ṭabāhu* means: called it. Passion and pasture cannot literally call, but since in them there is something that attracts, they became callers figuratively. It was also said: ﴿تَدْعُو﴾ ("calls") means: the guardians of Hell, whose calling is attributed to it.

﴿مَن أدْبَرَ﴾ ("whoever turned his back") from the truth, ﴿وتَوَلّى﴾ ("and turned away"), ﴿وجَمَعَ فَأوْعى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded"): that is, gathered wealth, placed it in a container, hoarded it, and did not pay God's right in it. This is an indication of wealthy disbelievers. Al-Hakim said: ʿAbdullah ibn Hakim would not tie up his purse, and he said: I heard God say: ﴿وجَمَعَ فَأوْعى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded").

﴿إنَّ الإنْسانَ﴾ ("Indeed, man") is a generic noun, and for this reason an exception is made from it: ﴿إلّا المُصَلِّينَ﴾ ("except those who pray"). It was also said: the reference is to the disbelievers. Tha'lab said: Muhammad ibn ʿAbdullah ibn Tahir said to me: What is *al-halaʿ* (anxiety)? I said: God has already explained it, and there can be no explanation clearer than His explanation, which is: when evil reaches him he shows extreme distress, and when good reaches him he is stingy with it and withholds it from people. End of quotation.

Since extreme distress and withholding are firmly established in man, it is as if he were created carried upon them, like His words: ﴿خُلِقَ الإنْسانُ مِن عَجَلٍ﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 37] ("Man was created of haste"). And *al-khayr* ("good") means wealth.

﴿إلّا المُصَلِّينَ﴾ ("except those who pray"): an exception from "man", as we have said; for this reason He described them with what He described them, namely patience under hardships, and the beautiful attributes which they practise. The majority read ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ﴾ ("over their prayer") in the singular; al-Hasan read it in the plural. And *daymūmatuhā* ("constancy in it"): the majority said: persistence in it. Ibn Mas'ud said: its performance at its time. ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir said: they remain in it and do not turn right or left, and from this comes "lasting wealth". Al-Zamakhshari said: their constancy in it is that they persist in performing it and do not occupy themselves away from it with anything; and their guarding of it is that they observe the completion of the ablution for it and its times, and they establish its pillars and complete it with its sunnas and its performance, and they protect it from being nullified by the sins that accompany it; and constancy returns to the prayers themselves and to the guarding of their states. End of quotation. This is his answer to the question: (If you say): how did He say ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ دائِمُونَ﴾ ("who are constant in their prayer") and then say ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ يُحافِظُونَ﴾ ("who guard their prayer")? I say: constancy in a thing and guarding it are one thing; but since prayer is the pillar of Islam, emphasis was carried to the utmost in it, so it was mentioned first and last among the qualities of Islam mentioned in this surah, to make known its rank among the pillars upon which Islam is built. The attributes that come after these have already been explained, and most of them are in Surat Qad Aflaha al-Mu'minun ("The believers have prospered"). The majority read ﴿بِشَهادَتِهِمْ﴾ ("in their testimonies") in the singular. Al-Sulami, Abu ʿAmr and Hafs read it in the plural.

﴿ذِي المَعارِجِ﴾: *al-ma'arij* means ascents or stairways, and here it is a metaphor. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada said: in ranks, favours and praiseworthy attributes. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: *al-ma'arij* are the heavens, in which the angels ascend from one heaven to another. Al-Hasan said: they are the steps up to heaven. It was also said: *al-ma'arij* are the upper chambers, meaning that He made them for His friends in Paradise.

(﴿تَعْرُجُ﴾) The reading of the majority is with the *ta'* (feminine form). ʿAbdullah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Miqsam and Za'ida from al-A'mash read it with the *ya'* (masculine form). (﴿والرُّوحُ﴾, "and the Spirit") The majority said: it is Gabriel, singled out for mention as an honour, and it is placed after the angels here, whereas it is placed before them in His words: ﴿يَوْمَ يَقُومُ الرُّوحُ والمَلائِكَةُ صَفًّا﴾ [An-Naba': 38] ("On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks"). Mujahid said: they are angels who guard the angels who guard the children of Adam; the guarding angels do not see them, just as we do not see our guardians. It was also said: the Spirit is an angel other than Gabriel, of great size. Abu Salih said: a creation in the form of humans, but they are not humans. Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb said: it is the spirit of the dead person at the moment it is taken. The pronoun ﴿إلَيْهِ﴾ ("to Him") refers to Allah, i.e. to His Throne, and to where His command descends from. It was also said: ﴿إلَيْهِ﴾ means to the place where they dwell, which is in the heaven, since it is the place of His goodness and honour. The apparent meaning is that they ascend in a day of your days, and the measure of the distance, if a human were to ascend it, is fifty thousand years. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Ishaq, and a group of the skilled scholars, among them the judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id. If the one ascending is an angel, Mujahid said: the distance is from the bottom of the seventh earth to the Throne. And whoever takes the Spirit to be a class of living creatures said: Wahb said: the distance is from the surface of the earth to the farthest end of the Throne. ʿIkrima and al-Hakam said: He meant the duration of this world, for it is fifty thousand years, and no one knows how much of it has passed and how much remains; that is, they ascend within the span of the world and the continuance of this structure. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: it is the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: its length is that number, and this is the apparent meaning of what has come in the hadith about the one who withholds zakat, for he said: "On a day whose measure is fifty thousand years." Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: He determined it, in its calamities, its terror and its severity, to be that number for the disbelievers. A hadith says: "It will be light for the believer, until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer." ʿIkrima said: the measure of the time in which the reckoning is concluded is the amount of time that would be needed to judge with justice over fifty thousand years of the days of this world. Al-Hasan said something similar. It was also said: the number is not meant literally; what is meant is the length of the standing on the Day of Resurrection and the hardships therein. The Arabs describe days of hardship as long, and days of joy as short. A poet describing days of joy and happiness said:

"And a day that, like the shadow of a spear, its length was shortened by the blood of the wineskin and the clashing of the lutes."

The apparent view is that His words "in a day" are connected to (﴿تَعْرُجُ﴾, "ascend"). It was also said that they are connected to (﴿دافِعٍ﴾, "averter"), and the clause "ascend" is a parenthetical insertion. Since they had asked for the hastening of the punishment, and that asking was in the manner of mockery and denial, and they had been promised it, He commanded him to be patient. As for the one who took (﴿سَألَ سائِلٌ﴾, "asked") to mean "flowing", the meaning is that it has come close to occurring. The pronoun in ﴿يَرَوْنَهُ﴾ ("they see it") refers to the punishment, or to the day if it is meant to be the Day of Resurrection. This regarding it as far away is, on their part, a form of denial by way of impossibility.

﴿ونَراهُ قَرِيبًا﴾ ("and We see it near"): that is, easy for Our power, not far from Us and not unattainable. Everything that is coming is near. Nearness and farness here concern possibility, not distance.

﴿يَوْمَ تَكُونُ﴾ ("on a day when it will be"): it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: it occurs on the day when ... ; or (﴿يَوْمَ تَكُونُ السَّماءُ كالمُهْلِ﴾, "on the day when the sky will be like molten brass") is such-and-such; or it is governed by (﴿قَرِيبًا﴾, "near"); or it is a substitute for the pronoun in "We see it" if that refers to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is a substitute for "in a day" according to the one who connected it to (﴿واقِعٍ﴾, "befalling"). End of quotation. This is not permissible, because "in a day", although it is in a position of accusative, cannot have an accusative substitute, since this is not among the positions which are observed in following words (*tawabi'*), for the preposition in it is not superfluous, nor is it treated as superfluous like *rubba*. The observance of position is only permitted with a superfluous preposition, as in the poem:

"O sons of Lubayna, you are not [a fist] in hand, except a hand that has no arm."

For this reason it is not permitted to say: "I passed by Zayd the tailor," observing the position of "by Zayd"; nor "I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr," nor "I was angry at Zayd and Jaʿfar," nor "I passed by ʿAmr, your brother," observing the position. (If you say): the vowel on *yawma* ("day") is a vowel of construction (*bina'*), not a vowel of grammatical inflection (*i'rab*), so it is in the genitive like "in a day." (I reply): its construction is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans, because it is attached to an inflected noun; but it is permitted according to the school of the Kufans. Al-Zamakhshari's statement would then be consistent with their school, if he had this in mind and intended it.

(﴿كالمُهْلِ﴾, "like molten brass") The discussion of it has already passed in Surat al-Dukhan. ﴿وتَكُونُ الجِبالُ كالعِهْنِ المَنفُوشِ﴾ [Al-Qari'a: 5] ("And the mountains will be like fluffed wool") as in al-Qari'a: when they are blown away, they fly in the air like fluffed wool when the wind scatters it. Al-Hasan said: the mountains move with the winds, then they crumble, then they become like wool, then they are blown away and become scattered dust.

The majority read (﴿ولا يَسْألُ﴾, "and no close friend will ask") in the active form, meaning: he will not ask him for help or benefit, knowing that he will not find that with him. Qatada said: he will not ask him about his condition, because it is evident. It was also said: he will not ask him to bear for him any part of his burdens, for he has despaired of that. It was also said: intercession. It was also said: *ḥamīman* ("a close friend") is in the accusative by the removal of *ʿan* ("about"), meaning: about a close friend, because of his preoccupation with what he is in.

Abu Haywa, Shayba, Abu Ja'far and al-Bazzi, with some difference of transmission from these three, read it in the passive form, meaning: he will not be asked to bring him, since each of the believer and the disbeliever has a sign by which he is recognized. It was also said: he will not be asked about the sins of his close friend, so that he may be taken to account for them.

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ ("they will be made to see them"): a resumption of speech. Ibn ʿAbbas said: on the gathering-place, the close friend sees his close friend, then he flees from him because of his preoccupation with himself. It was also said: they are made to see them in the Fire. It was also said: they are made to see them, so they have no need to ask or to request. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that "they are made to see them" is a qualifying clause, meaning: close friends who are made to see one another, turning them away. End of quotation. ﴿حَمِيمٌ حَمِيمًا﴾ ("close friend ... close friend"): both are indefinite nouns in a negative context, so they are general, and for this reason the pronoun was made plural. Qatada read ﴿يُبْصِرُونَهم﴾ ("they make them see") with *tashdid* removed and with the *ṣad* vowelled with kasra, meaning: the believer sees the disbeliever in the Fire; this was said by Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: the disbeliever sees the one who misled him in the Fire, as a lesson, as vengeance, and as grief.

﴿يَوَدُّ المُجْرِمُ﴾ ("the guilty one would wish"): that is, the disbeliever, though it may include the sinful believer who is punished. The majority read *min ʿadhābi* as an idafa (construct). Abu Haywa read it with *fatḥa* on the final vowel. (﴿وصاحِبَتِهِ﴾, "and his spouse") his wife. (﴿وفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾, "and his close kin") his nearest relatives. (﴿تُؤْوِيهِ﴾, "that shelters him") that takes him in, by belonging to it, or seeking refuge with it in calamities.

﴿ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ ("and then rescues him") is conjoined to (﴿يَفْتَدِي﴾, "would ransom himself"), meaning: rescues him by ransoming, or the ones mentioned before. Al-Zuhri read *tu'wīhi* and *tunjīhi* with both *hā'*s vowelled with *ḍamma*. (﴿كَلّا﴾, "No!") a rebuke to their wish to ransom themselves, and an alert that it will not benefit. (﴿إنَّها﴾, "Indeed it") the pronoun refers to the matter (the story), and ﴿لَظى نَزّاعَةً﴾ ("the Blaze, plucking out") is an explanation of it, or of the Fire, which is indicated by the word *ʿadhāb* ("punishment") in ﴿عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ﴾ ("the punishment of that day"). ﴿لَظى﴾ ("the Blaze") is a substitute for the pronoun, and ﴿نَزّاعَةً﴾ ("plucking out") is the predicate of *inna*, or the predicate of an inchoative, and ﴿لَظى﴾ is the predicate of *inna*, meaning: it is plucking out; or it is a substitute for ﴿لَظى﴾, or a predicate after a predicate. All of this has been mentioned, on the reading of the majority with the *rafʿ* ("nominative") of "plucking out". Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that it be an ambiguous pronoun explained by the predicate. End of quotation. I do not know what this hidden pronoun is that the predicate explains; this is not one of the positions in which a single noun explains a pronoun. Were it not that he mentioned after this "or the pronoun of the matter", I would have interpreted his words in that sense. Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Haywa, al-Za'farani, Ibn Miqsam, Hafs, and al-Yazidi in his selection read "plucking out" with *naṣb* ("accusative"). Then it is fixed that ﴿لَظى﴾ is the predicate of *inna*, and the pronoun in *innahā* refers to the Fire which is indicated by "punishment". "Plucking out" is in the accusative as a qualifying state, either emphasizing or specifying, and the element governing it is ﴿لَظى﴾, although it governs it only insofar as there is in it the sense of blazing, just as the proper name governs the adverb in the poet's words:

"I am Abu al-Minhal, at times."

That is: famous at times. Or it is in the accusative of specification for exaggeration (*li-l-tahwīl*); this was said by al-Zamakhshari, and he seems to mean the cutting-off (of the qualifier). So the accusative in it is like the nominative in it, if you supply "he" as a pronoun, so you supply it here, I mean "calls", that is: in reality God creates in it speech, just as He creates it in the limbs; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and others, "calling them by their names and their fathers' names". Al-Zamakhshari said: and as He created it in the tree. End of quotation. He thus did not abandon the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). Al-Khalil said: it is a metaphor for its summoning them, and what it inflicts on them of its punishment. Tha'lab said: it destroys; the Arabs say: *daʿā Allāhu*, meaning: God destroyed you; al-Khalil related this from the Arabs. The poet said:

"Nights when passion calls me, and I answer it, and the eyes of the one I love look at me with tenderness."

And another said:

"It rose up to be seen, and every wide path was made dear to it by pasture and open land."

He describes an ostrich; *ṭabāhu* means: called it. Passion and pasture cannot literally call, but since in them there is something that attracts, they became callers figuratively. It was also said: ﴿تَدْعُو﴾ ("calls") means: the guardians of Hell, whose calling is attributed to it.

﴿مَن أدْبَرَ﴾ ("whoever turned his back") from the truth, ﴿وتَوَلّى﴾ ("and turned away"), ﴿وجَمَعَ فَأوْعى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded"): that is, gathered wealth, placed it in a container, hoarded it, and did not pay God's right in it. This is an indication of wealthy disbelievers. Al-Hakim said: ʿAbdullah ibn Hakim would not tie up his purse, and he said: I heard God say: ﴿وجَمَعَ فَأوْعى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded").

﴿إنَّ الإنْسانَ﴾ ("Indeed, man") is a generic noun, and for this reason an exception is made from it: ﴿إلّا المُصَلِّينَ﴾ ("except those who pray"). It was also said: the reference is to the disbelievers. Tha'lab said: Muhammad ibn ʿAbdullah ibn Tahir said to me: What is *al-halaʿ* (anxiety)? I said: God has already explained it, and there can be no explanation clearer than His explanation, which is: when evil reaches him he shows extreme distress, and when good reaches him he is stingy with it and withholds it from people. End of quotation.

Since extreme distress and withholding are firmly established in man, it is as if he were created carried upon them, like His words: ﴿خُلِقَ الإنْسانُ مِن عَجَلٍ﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 37] ("Man was created of haste"). And *al-khayr* ("good") means wealth.

﴿إلّا المُصَلِّينَ﴾ ("except those who pray"): an exception from "man", as we have said; for this reason He described them with what He described them, namely patience under hardships, and the beautiful attributes which they practise. The majority read ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ﴾ ("over their prayer") in the singular; al-Hasan read it in the plural. And *daymūmatuhā* ("constancy in it"): the majority said: persistence in it. Ibn Mas'ud said: its performance at its time. ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir said: they remain in it and do not turn right or left, and from this comes "lasting wealth". Al-Zamakhshari said: their constancy in it is that they persist in performing it and do not occupy themselves away from it with anything; and their guarding of it is that they observe the completion of the ablution for it and its times, and they establish its pillars and complete it with its sunnas and its performance, and they protect it from being nullified by the sins that accompany it; and constancy returns to the prayers themselves and to the guarding of their states. End of quotation. This is his answer to the question: (If you say): how did He say ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ دائِمُونَ﴾ ("who are constant in their prayer") and then say ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ يُحافِظُونَ﴾ ("who guard their prayer")? I say: constancy in a thing and guarding it are one thing; but since prayer is the pillar of Islam, emphasis was carried to the utmost in it, so it was mentioned first and last among the qualities of Islam mentioned in this surah, to make known its rank among the pillars upon which Islam is built. The attributes that come after these have already been explained, and most of them are in Surat Qad Aflaha al-Mu'minun ("The believers have prospered"). The majority read ﴿بِشَهادَتِهِمْ﴾ ("in their testimonies") in the singular. Al-Sulami, Abu ʿAmr and Hafs read it in the plural.

﴿ذِي المَعارِجِ﴾: *al-ma'arij* means ascents or stairways, and here it is a metaphor. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada said: in ranks, favours and praiseworthy attributes. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: *al-ma'arij* are the heavens, in which the angels ascend from one heaven to another. Al-Hasan said: they are the steps up to heaven. It was also said: *al-ma'arij* are the upper chambers, meaning that He made them for His friends in Paradise.

(﴿تَعْرُجُ﴾) The reading of the majority is with the *ta'* (feminine form). ʿAbdullah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Miqsam and Za'ida from al-A'mash read it with the *ya'* (masculine form). (﴿والرُّوحُ﴾, "and the Spirit") The majority said: it is Gabriel, singled out for mention as an honour, and it is placed after the angels here, whereas it is placed before them in His words: ﴿يَوْمَ يَقُومُ الرُّوحُ والمَلائِكَةُ صَفًّا﴾ [An-Naba': 38] ("On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks"). Mujahid said: they are angels who guard the angels who guard the children of Adam; the guarding angels do not see them, just as we do not see our guardians. It was also said: the Spirit is an angel other than Gabriel, of great size. Abu Salih said: a creation in the form of humans, but they are not humans. Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb said: it is the spirit of the dead person at the moment it is taken. The pronoun ﴿إلَيْهِ﴾ ("to Him") refers to Allah, i.e. to His Throne, and to where His command descends from. It was also said: ﴿إلَيْهِ﴾ means to the place where they dwell, which is in the heaven, since it is the place of His goodness and honour. The apparent meaning is that they ascend in a day of your days, and the measure of the distance, if a human were to ascend it, is fifty thousand years. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Ishaq, and a group of the skilled scholars, among them the judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id. If the one ascending is an angel, Mujahid said: the distance is from the bottom of the seventh earth to the Throne. And whoever takes the Spirit to be a class of living creatures said: Wahb said: the distance is from the surface of the earth to the farthest end of the Throne. ʿIkrima and al-Hakam said: He meant the duration of this world, for it is fifty thousand years, and no one knows how much of it has passed and how much remains; that is, they ascend within the span of the world and the continuance of this structure. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: it is the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: its length is that number, and this is the apparent meaning of what has come in the hadith about the one who withholds zakat, for he said: "On a day whose measure is fifty thousand years." Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: He determined it, in its calamities, its terror and its severity, to be that number for the disbelievers. A hadith says: "It will be light for the believer, until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer." ʿIkrima said: the measure of the time in which the reckoning is concluded is the amount of time that would be needed to judge with justice over fifty thousand years of the days of this world. Al-Hasan said something similar. It was also said: the number is not meant literally; what is meant is the length of the standing on the Day of Resurrection and the hardships therein. The Arabs describe days of hardship as long, and days of joy as short. A poet describing days of joy and happiness said:

"And a day that, like the shadow of a spear, its length was shortened by the blood of the wineskin and the clashing of the lutes."

The apparent view is that His words "in a day" are connected to (﴿تَعْرُجُ﴾, "ascend"). It was also said that they are connected to (﴿دافِعٍ﴾, "averter"), and the clause "ascend" is a parenthetical insertion. Since they had asked for the hastening of the punishment, and that asking was in the manner of mockery and denial, and they had been promised it, He commanded him to be patient. As for the one who took (﴿سَألَ سائِلٌ﴾, "asked") to mean "flowing", the meaning is that it has come close to occurring. The pronoun in ﴿يَرَوْنَهُ﴾ ("they see it") refers to the punishment, or to the day if it is meant to be the Day of Resurrection. This regarding it as far away is, on their part, a form of denial by way of impossibility.

﴿ونَراهُ قَرِيبًا﴾ ("and We see it near"): that is, easy for Our power, not far from Us and not unattainable. Everything that is coming is near. Nearness and farness here concern possibility, not distance.

﴿يَوْمَ تَكُونُ﴾ ("on a day when it will be"): it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: it occurs on the day when ... ; or (﴿يَوْمَ تَكُونُ السَّماءُ كالمُهْلِ﴾, "on the day when the sky will be like molten brass") is such-and-such; or it is governed by (﴿قَرِيبًا﴾, "near"); or it is a substitute for the pronoun in "We see it" if that refers to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is a substitute for "in a day" according to the one who connected it to (﴿واقِعٍ﴾, "befalling"). End of quotation. This is not permissible, because "in a day", although it is in a position of accusative, cannot have an accusative substitute, since this is not among the positions which are observed in following words (*tawabi'*), for the preposition in it is not superfluous, nor is it treated as superfluous like *rubba*. The observance of position is only permitted with a superfluous preposition, as in the poem:

"O sons of Lubayna, you are not [a fist] in hand, except a hand that has no arm."

For this reason it is not permitted to say: "I passed by Zayd the tailor," observing the position of "by Zayd"; nor "I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr," nor "I was angry at Zayd and Jaʿfar," nor "I passed by ʿAmr, your brother," observing the position. (If you say): the vowel on *yawma* ("day") is a vowel of construction (*bina'*), not a vowel of grammatical inflection (*i'rab*), so it is in the genitive like "in a day." (I reply): its construction is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans, because it is attached to an inflected noun; but it is permitted according to the school of the Kufans. Al-Zamakhshari's statement would then be consistent with their school, if he had this in mind and intended it.

(﴿كالمُهْلِ﴾, "like molten brass") The discussion of it has already passed in Surat al-Dukhan. ﴿وتَكُونُ الجِبالُ كالعِهْنِ المَنفُوشِ﴾ [Al-Qari'a: 5] ("And the mountains will be like fluffed wool") as in al-Qari'a: when they are blown away, they fly in the air like fluffed wool when the wind scatters it. Al-Hasan said: the mountains move with the winds, then they crumble, then they become like wool, then they are blown away and become scattered dust.

The majority read (﴿ولا يَسْألُ﴾, "and no close friend will ask") in the active form, meaning: he will not ask him for help or benefit, knowing that he will not find that with him. Qatada said: he will not ask him about his condition, because it is evident. It was also said: he will not ask him to bear for him any part of his burdens, for he has despaired of that. It was also said: intercession. It was also said: *ḥamīman* ("a close friend") is in the accusative by the removal of *ʿan* ("about"), meaning: about a close friend, because of his preoccupation with what he is in.

Abu Haywa, Shayba, Abu Ja'far and al-Bazzi, with some difference of transmission from these three, read it in the passive form, meaning: he will not be asked to bring him, since each of the believer and the disbeliever has a sign by which he is recognized. It was also said: he will not be asked about the sins of his close friend, so that he may be taken to account for them.

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ ("they will be made to see them"): a resumption of speech. Ibn ʿAbbas said: on the gathering-place, the close friend sees his close friend, then he flees from him because of his preoccupation with himself. It was also said: they are made to see them in the Fire. It was also said: they are made to see them, so they have no need to ask or to request. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that "they are made to see them" is a qualifying clause, meaning: close friends who are made to see one another, turning them away. End of quotation. ﴿حَمِيمٌ حَمِيمًا﴾ ("close friend ... close friend"): both are indefinite nouns in a negative context, so they are general, and for this reason the pronoun was made plural. Qatada read ﴿يُبْصِرُونَهم﴾ ("they make them see") with *tashdid* removed and with the *ṣad* vowelled with kasra, meaning: the believer sees the disbeliever in the Fire; this was said by Mujahid. Ibn Zayd said: the disbeliever sees the one who misled him in the Fire, as a lesson, as vengeance, and as grief.

﴿يَوَدُّ المُجْرِمُ﴾ ("the guilty one would wish"): that is, the disbeliever, though it may include the sinful believer who is punished. The majority read *min ʿadhābi* as an idafa (construct). Abu Haywa read it with *fatḥa* on the final vowel. (﴿وصاحِبَتِهِ﴾, "and his spouse") his wife. (﴿وفَصِيلَتِهِ﴾, "and his close kin") his nearest relatives. (﴿تُؤْوِيهِ﴾, "that shelters him") that takes him in, by belonging to it, or seeking refuge with it in calamities.

﴿ثُمَّ يُنْجِيهِ﴾ ("and then rescues him") is conjoined to (﴿يَفْتَدِي﴾, "would ransom himself"), meaning: rescues him by ransoming, or the ones mentioned before. Al-Zuhri read *tu'wīhi* and *tunjīhi* with both *hā'*s vowelled with *ḍamma*. (﴿كَلّا﴾, "No!") a rebuke to their wish to ransom themselves, and an alert that it will not benefit. (﴿إنَّها﴾, "Indeed it") the pronoun refers to the matter (the story), and ﴿لَظى نَزّاعَةً﴾ ("the Blaze, plucking out") is an explanation of it, or of the Fire, which is indicated by the word *ʿadhāb* ("punishment") in ﴿عَذابِ يَوْمِئِذٍ﴾ ("the punishment of that day"). ﴿لَظى﴾ ("the Blaze") is a substitute for the pronoun, and ﴿نَزّاعَةً﴾ ("plucking out") is the predicate of *inna*, or the predicate of an inchoative, and ﴿لَظى﴾ is the predicate of *inna*, meaning: it is plucking out; or it is a substitute for ﴿لَظى﴾, or a predicate after a predicate. All of this has been mentioned, on the reading of the majority with the *rafʿ* ("nominative") of "plucking out". Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that it be an ambiguous pronoun explained by the predicate. End of quotation. I do not know what this hidden pronoun is that the predicate explains; this is not one of the positions in which a single noun explains a pronoun. Were it not that he mentioned after this "or the pronoun of the matter", I would have interpreted his words in that sense. Ibn Abi ʿAbla, Abu Haywa, al-Za'farani, Ibn Miqsam, Hafs, and al-Yazidi in his selection read "plucking out" with *naṣb* ("accusative"). Then it is fixed that ﴿لَظى﴾ is the predicate of *inna*, and the pronoun in *innahā* refers to the Fire which is indicated by "punishment". "Plucking out" is in the accusative as a qualifying state, either emphasizing or specifying, and the element governing it is ﴿لَظى﴾, although it governs it only insofar as there is in it the sense of blazing, just as the proper name governs the adverb in the poet's words:

"I am Abu al-Minhal, at times."

That is: famous at times. Or it is in the accusative of specification for exaggeration (*li-l-tahwīl*); this was said by al-Zamakhshari, and he seems to mean the cutting-off (of the qualifier). So the accusative in it is like the nominative in it, if you supply "he" as a pronoun, so you supply it here, I mean "calls", that is: in reality God creates in it speech, just as He creates it in the limbs; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and others, "calling them by their names and their fathers' names". Al-Zamakhshari said: and as He created it in the tree. End of quotation. He thus did not abandon the doctrine of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). Al-Khalil said: it is a metaphor for its summoning them, and what it inflicts on them of its punishment. Tha'lab said: it destroys; the Arabs say: *daʿā Allāhu*, meaning: God destroyed you; al-Khalil related this from the Arabs. The poet said:

"Nights when passion calls me, and I answer it, and the eyes of the one I love look at me with tenderness."

And another said:

"It rose up to be seen, and every wide path was made dear to it by pasture and open land."

He describes an ostrich; *ṭabāhu* means: called it. Passion and pasture cannot literally call, but since in them there is something that attracts, they became callers figuratively. It was also said: ﴿تَدْعُو﴾ ("calls") means: the guardians of Hell, whose calling is attributed to it.

﴿مَن أدْبَرَ﴾ ("whoever turned his back") from the truth, ﴿وتَوَلّى﴾ ("and turned away"), ﴿وجَمَعَ فَأوْعى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded"): that is, gathered wealth, placed it in a container, hoarded it, and did not pay God's right in it. This is an indication of wealthy disbelievers. Al-Hakim said: ʿAbdullah ibn Hakim would not tie up his purse, and he said: I heard God say: ﴿وجَمَعَ فَأوْعى﴾ ("and gathered and hoarded").

﴿إنَّ الإنْسانَ﴾ ("Indeed, man") is a generic noun, and for this reason an exception is made from it: ﴿إلّا المُصَلِّينَ﴾ ("except those who pray"). It was also said: the reference is to the disbelievers. Tha'lab said: Muhammad ibn ʿAbdullah ibn Tahir said to me: What is *al-halaʿ* (anxiety)? I said: God has already explained it, and there can be no explanation clearer than His explanation, which is: when evil reaches him he shows extreme distress, and when good reaches him he is stingy with it and withholds it from people. End of quotation.

Since extreme distress and withholding are firmly established in man, it is as if he were created carried upon them, like His words: ﴿خُلِقَ الإنْسانُ مِن عَجَلٍ﴾ [Al-Anbiya': 37] ("Man was created of haste"). And *al-khayr* ("good") means wealth.

﴿إلّا المُصَلِّينَ﴾ ("except those who pray"): an exception from "man", as we have said; for this reason He described them with what He described them, namely patience under hardships, and the beautiful attributes which they practise. The majority read ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ﴾ ("over their prayer") in the singular; al-Hasan read it in the plural. And *daymūmatuhā* ("constancy in it"): the majority said: persistence in it. Ibn Mas'ud said: its performance at its time. ʿUqba ibn ʿAmir said: they remain in it and do not turn right or left, and from this comes "lasting wealth". Al-Zamakhshari said: their constancy in it is that they persist in performing it and do not occupy themselves away from it with anything; and their guarding of it is that they observe the completion of the ablution for it and its times, and they establish its pillars and complete it with its sunnas and its performance, and they protect it from being nullified by the sins that accompany it; and constancy returns to the prayers themselves and to the guarding of their states. End of quotation. This is his answer to the question: (If you say): how did He say ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ دائِمُونَ﴾ ("who are constant in their prayer") and then say ﴿عَلى صَلاتِهِمْ يُحافِظُونَ﴾ ("who guard their prayer")? I say: constancy in a thing and guarding it are one thing; but since prayer is the pillar of Islam, emphasis was carried to the utmost in it, so it was mentioned first and last among the qualities of Islam mentioned in this surah, to make known its rank among the pillars upon which Islam is built. The attributes that come after these have already been explained, and most of them are in Surat Qad Aflaha al-Mu'minun ("The believers have prospered"). The majority read ﴿بِشَهادَتِهِمْ﴾ ("in their testimonies") in the singular. Al-Sulami, Abu ʿAmr and Hafs read it in the plural.

﴿ذِي المَعارِجِ﴾: *al-ma'arij* means ascents or stairways, and here it is a metaphor. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatada said: in ranks, favours and praiseworthy attributes. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: *al-ma'arij* are the heavens, in which the angels ascend from one heaven to another. Al-Hasan said: they are the steps up to heaven. It was also said: *al-ma'arij* are the upper chambers, meaning that He made them for His friends in Paradise.

(﴿تَعْرُجُ﴾) The reading of the majority is with the *ta'* (feminine form). ʿAbdullah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Miqsam and Za'ida from al-A'mash read it with the *ya'* (masculine form). (﴿والرُّوحُ﴾, "and the Spirit") The majority said: it is Gabriel, singled out for mention as an honour, and it is placed after the angels here, whereas it is placed before them in His words: ﴿يَوْمَ يَقُومُ الرُّوحُ والمَلائِكَةُ صَفًّا﴾ [An-Naba': 38] ("On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in ranks"). Mujahid said: they are angels who guard the angels who guard the children of Adam; the guarding angels do not see them, just as we do not see our guardians. It was also said: the Spirit is an angel other than Gabriel, of great size. Abu Salih said: a creation in the form of humans, but they are not humans. Qabisa ibn Dhu'ayb said: it is the spirit of the dead person at the moment it is taken. The pronoun ﴿إلَيْهِ﴾ ("to Him") refers to Allah, i.e. to His Throne, and to where His command descends from. It was also said: ﴿إلَيْهِ﴾ means to the place where they dwell, which is in the heaven, since it is the place of His goodness and honour. The apparent meaning is that they ascend in a day of your days, and the measure of the distance, if a human were to ascend it, is fifty thousand years. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn Ishaq, and a group of the skilled scholars, among them the judge Mundhir ibn Sa'id. If the one ascending is an angel, Mujahid said: the distance is from the bottom of the seventh earth to the Throne. And whoever takes the Spirit to be a class of living creatures said: Wahb said: the distance is from the surface of the earth to the farthest end of the Throne. ʿIkrima and al-Hakam said: He meant the duration of this world, for it is fifty thousand years, and no one knows how much of it has passed and how much remains; that is, they ascend within the span of the world and the continuance of this structure. Ibn ʿAbbas also said: it is the Day of Resurrection. It was also said: its length is that number, and this is the apparent meaning of what has come in the hadith about the one who withholds zakat, for he said: "On a day whose measure is fifty thousand years." Ibn ʿAbbas and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri said: He determined it, in its calamities, its terror and its severity, to be that number for the disbelievers. A hadith says: "It will be light for the believer, until it is lighter for him than an obligatory prayer." ʿIkrima said: the measure of the time in which the reckoning is concluded is the amount of time that would be needed to judge with justice over fifty thousand years of the days of this world. Al-Hasan said something similar. It was also said: the number is not meant literally; what is meant is the length of the standing on the Day of Resurrection and the hardships therein. The Arabs describe days of hardship as long, and days of joy as short. A poet describing days of joy and happiness said:

"And a day that, like the shadow of a spear, its length was shortened by the blood of the wineskin and the clashing of the lutes."

The apparent view is that His words "in a day" are connected to (﴿تَعْرُجُ﴾, "ascend"). It was also said that they are connected to (﴿دافِعٍ﴾, "averter"), and the clause "ascend" is a parenthetical insertion. Since they had asked for the hastening of the punishment, and that asking was in the manner of mockery and denial, and they had been promised it, He commanded him to be patient. As for the one who took (﴿سَألَ سائِلٌ﴾, "asked") to mean "flowing", the meaning is that it has come close to occurring. The pronoun in ﴿يَرَوْنَهُ﴾ ("they see it") refers to the punishment, or to the day if it is meant to be the Day of Resurrection. This regarding it as far away is, on their part, a form of denial by way of impossibility.

﴿ونَراهُ قَرِيبًا﴾ ("and We see it near"): that is, easy for Our power, not far from Us and not unattainable. Everything that is coming is near. Nearness and farness here concern possibility, not distance.

﴿يَوْمَ تَكُونُ﴾ ("on a day when it will be"): it is in the accusative by an implied verb, meaning: it occurs on the day when ... ; or (﴿يَوْمَ تَكُونُ السَّماءُ كالمُهْلِ﴾, "on the day when the sky will be like molten brass") is such-and-such; or it is governed by (﴿قَرِيبًا﴾, "near"); or it is a substitute for the pronoun in "We see it" if that refers to the Day of Resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari said: or it is a substitute for "in a day" according to the one who connected it to (﴿واقِعٍ﴾, "befalling"). End of quotation. This is not permissible, because "in a day", although it is in a position of accusative, cannot have an accusative substitute, since this is not among the positions which are observed in following words (*tawabi'*), for the preposition in it is not superfluous, nor is it treated as superfluous like *rubba*. The observance of position is only permitted with a superfluous preposition, as in the poem:

"O sons of Lubayna, you are not [a fist] in hand, except a hand that has no arm."

For this reason it is not permitted to say: "I passed by Zayd the tailor," observing the position of "by Zayd"; nor "I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr," nor "I was angry at Zayd and Jaʿfar," nor "I passed by ʿAmr, your brother," observing the position. (If you say): the vowel on *yawma* ("day") is a vowel of construction (*bina'*), not a vowel of grammatical inflection (*i'rab*), so it is in the genitive like "in a day." (I reply): its construction is not permitted according to the school of the Basrans, because it is attached to an inflected noun; but it is permitted according to the school of the Kufans. Al-Zamakhshari's statement would then be consistent with their school, if he had this in mind and intended it.

(﴿كالمُهْلِ﴾, "like molten brass") The discussion of it has already passed in Surat al-Dukhan. ﴿وتَكُونُ الجِبالُ كالعِهْنِ المَنفُوشِ﴾ [Al-Qari'a: 5] ("And the mountains will be like fluffed wool") as in al-Qari'a: when they are blown away, they fly in the air like fluffed wool when the wind scatters it. Al-Hasan said: the mountains move with the winds, then they crumble, then they become like wool, then they are blown away and become scattered dust.

The majority read (﴿ولا يَسْألُ﴾, "and no close friend will ask") in the active form, meaning: he will not ask him for help or benefit, knowing that he will not find that with him. Qatada said: he will not ask him about his condition, because it is evident. It was also said: he will not ask him to bear for him any part of his burdens, for he has despaired of that. It was also said: intercession. It was also said: *ḥamīman* ("a close friend") is in the accusative by the removal of *ʿan* ("about"), meaning: about a close friend, because of his preoccupation with what he is in.

Abu Haywa, Shayba, Abu Ja'far and al-Bazzi, with some difference of transmission from these three, read it in the passive form, meaning: he will not be asked to bring him, since each of the believer and the disbeliever has a sign by which he is recognized. It was also said: he will not be asked about the sins of his close friend, so that he may be taken to account for them.

﴿يُبَصَّرُونَهُمْ﴾ ("they will be made to see them"): a resumption of speech. Ibn ʿAbbas said: on the gathering-place, the close friend sees his close friend, then he flees from him because of his preoccupation with himself. It was also said: they are made to see them in the Fire. It was also said: they are made to see them, so they have no need to ask or to request. Al-Zamakhshari said: it is permissible that "they are made to see them" is a qualifying clause, meaning: close friends who are made to see one another, turning them away. End of quotation. ﴿حَمِيمٌ حَمِيمًا﴾ ("close friend ... close friend"): both are indefinite nouns in a negative context, so they are general, and for this reason the pronoun was made plural.
